sentences.text: The only known species, Qiupanykus zhangi, was named in honor of Shuancheng Zhang, who helped find the fossils.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is a poorly preserved postcranial skeleton containing elements from all body regions, including cervical, sacral, and caudal vertebrae, parts of the pelvis, an articulated right hindlimb, foot digits, and three pedal claws.
Measurements of the leg bones show the femur was approximately 74.2 mm, the tibia 98.6 mm, and the longest metatarsal 75.4 mm, resulting in a fully extended leg length estimated at about 24.8 cm.
Estimates for the animal's size vary; based on isometric scaling, the mass was calculated at 0.52 kg, while subsequent studies suggested 0.58 kg or a possible range between 0.27 and 0.91 kg.
Scaling estimates place the mass of associated eggs at about 1136 g, which significantly exceeds the estimated body mass of the holotype individual.
This phenomenon mirrors how modern kiwis lay eggs that are 20% of the mother's mass, illustrating how miniaturization can lead to disproportionately large eggs.
Researchers suggest the large hand claws were used to break eggshells for feeding.

The fossils were found in the Tantou Basin within Luanchuan County, Henan Province, China, in strata dating to the end of the Maastrichtian stage, the final stage of the Mesozoic Era, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.

The holotype specimen, designated 41HIII-0101, is housed at the Henan Geological Museum in Zhengzhou, where it was formally described in 2018 by a team led by Lü Junchang in the journal of the Chinese Geological Survey.
The femur-to-tibia ratio and arctometatarsus — a specific foot structure — suggest Qiupanykus was a capable runner.
Researchers suggest Qiupanykus reflects a miniaturization event in alvarezsaurian evolution during the early-to-middle Cenomanian.

No skull remains are known, so feeding habits cannot be directly inferred from skull anatomy, but the unique hand morphology suggests alvarezsaurids may have specialized in feeding on colonial insects like ants.

Multiple authors suggest the associated egg ootaxon Arriagadoolithus may have been laid by Qiupanykus, though the eggshells resemble those attributed to oviraptorosaurs found elsewhere in the Qiupa Formation, and juvenile oviraptorosaur fossils found near Qiupanykus support the link between the eggs and oviraptorosaurs, even though the egg was likely too massive for the holotype individual to have laid, suggesting it belonged to a larger parent.

More complete fossil remains are known from small theropods in this area than from large dinosaurs, living alongside turtles, lizards like Tianyusaurus, small mammals, and the uniquely edentulous enantiornithine Yuornis.
Qiupanykus belongs to the parent group Alvarezsauroidea and is classified as a reptile.

Phylogenetic analysis places Qiupanykus at the base of Parvicursorinae in a polytomy with several other taxa; although not formally assigned to Parvicursorinae in its description, its phylogenetic position makes it a member of that clade, a conclusion reaffirmed by a 2024 study by Meso, Pol, and Makovicky.

Qiupanykus fossils were found in strata that correspond to the K-T boundary and the beginning of the Cenozoic era, deposited by a braided river delta in an area interpreted as having been a coastal environment at the end of the Cretaceous Period.
Some subsequent authors argue that the egg could still have belonged to Qiupanykus despite the size discrepancy.
